title: From As-Saffat to Al-Hadid
intro: 44 days through surahs 37 to 57, from As-Saffat to Al-Hadid, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: This plan walks through surahs 37 to 57, beginning with As-Saffat, "Those Who Set the Ranks", a Meccan surah of 182 verses. It opens with oaths by those who stand in ranks, whom many commentators understand as angels, then declares that Allah is One. "The sun's risings" renders al-mashariq, which commentators link to the sun rising at a different point through the year.

The last three verses of As-Saffat: glory to Allah, peace on His messengers, and praise to the Lord of the Worlds. Many Muslims recite them to close a prayer, a supplication or a gathering. "Those sent (to warn)" are the prophets whose stories fill the surah, from Nuh (Noah) to Yunus (Jonah).

Sad is a Meccan surah of 88 verses, named after the Arabic letter that opens it; 29 surahs open with such isolated letters. This verse gives a reason the Quran was revealed: so that people ponder it. The Arabic word is from the root of tadabbur, which Muslims still use for slow, reflective study of the Quran.

posts.display: When thy Lord said unto the angels: Lo! I am about to create a mortal out of mire, And when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My Spirit, then fall down before him prostrate.
posts.caption: Sad retells the creation of the Prophet Adam. Allah shapes a human from clay ("mire") and breathes into him of His Spirit, and the angels are told to bow before him, which commentators explain as a prostration of honour, not worship. All of them do, except Iblis, who refuses out of pride.

Az-Zumar, "The Troops", is a Meccan surah of 75 verses. Some classical commentators link "Allah's earth is spacious" to believers persecuted in Mecca, some of whom emigrated to Abyssinia. The steadfast, people of sabr (patient endurance), are promised a reward "without stint": beyond all counting.

Often called one of the most hopeful verses in the Quran. "Prodigal to their own hurt" means people who have wronged themselves through sin, and they are told not to despair of Allah's mercy. The very next verse calls them to turn back to Him in repentance, and commentators read the two together.

The last verse of Az-Zumar. The surah's name, "The Troops", comes from the verses just before this, where people are led in groups to their final homes. It ends with the angels around the Throne and the same words of praise that open the Quran in Al-Fatiha.

Ghafir means "The Forgiver", one of the names in this passage. It is a Meccan surah of 85 verses, also called Al-Mu'min ("The Believer"), and the first of seven surahs that open with the letters Ha Mim. The names here hold a balance: forgiving and accepting repentance, yet stern in punishment.

One of the Quran's clearest promises about prayer: call on Allah and He answers. The prayer meant is du'a, personal supplication, and refusing it is called scorning "My service", that is, worship. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported to have recited this verse after saying "supplication is worship".

Fussilat, "Explained in Detail", is a Meccan surah of 54 verses. "Upright" translates istaqamu: they stood firm and straight in their faith. Many commentators say the angels bring this comfort at the moment of death: no fear of what lies ahead, no grief for what is left behind.

A verse often quoted on handling conflict: answer a wrong with something better, and an enemy may become a "bosom friend", a close and warm one. The next verse adds that only the patient attain this, and those blessed with great good fortune.

Ash-Shura, "The Consultation", is a Meccan surah of 53 verses. "Naught is as His likeness" is one of the Quran's central statements about Allah: nothing in creation resembles Him. Yet the same verse calls Him the Hearer and the Seer, and theologians have long reflected on how the two fit together.

posts.display: And those who answer the call of their Lord and establish worship, and whose affairs are a matter of counsel, and who spend of what We have bestowed on them.
posts.caption: This verse gives the surah its name: believers whose affairs are settled by counsel, shura in Arabic. It is part of a longer portrait of the faithful that also includes trust in Allah, forgiving when angry, and patience. Muslims have long cited it on the value of mutual consultation.

posts.display: Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us, and we were not capable (of subduing them). And lo! unto our Lord we surely are returning.
posts.display_original: سُبْحَٰنَ ٱلَّذِى سَخَّرَ لَنَا هَٰذَا وَمَا كُنَّا لَهُۥ مُقْرِنِينَ وَإِنَّآ إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ
posts.caption: Az-Zukhruf, "Ornaments of Gold", is a Meccan surah of 89 verses. The verses just before speak of the ships and animals Allah gave people to ride, and "these" refers to them. Muslims recite these words as a supplication when setting out on a journey, now in cars, trains and planes too, and some commentators see in the last line a reminder of the final return to Allah.

A sobering picture of the Day of Judgment: friendships built on wrongdoing turn to blame and hostility. The exception is "those who kept their duty", the muttaqin, people of taqwa or mindfulness of Allah, whose friendship lasts beyond this life.

posts.display: By the Scripture that maketh plain - Lo! We revealed it on a blessed night - Lo! We are ever warning.
posts.caption: Ad-Dukhan, "The Smoke", is a Meccan surah of 59 verses. It opens by swearing by the Scripture that makes things plain, then says it was sent down on a blessed night. Most commentators identify that night with Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Decree in Ramadan, when the Quran was first sent down.

The universe was not made "in play", without purpose. The theme returns often in the Quran: creation is made "with truth", with meaning and an end in view, and human life is part of that purpose. Pickthall's "save" means "except".

posts.display: Allah it is Who hath made the sea of service unto you that the ships may run thereon by His command, and that ye may seek of His bounty, and that haply ye may be thankful.
posts.caption: Al-Jathiyah, "The Kneeling", is a Meccan surah of 37 verses, named for its image of every nation kneeling at the Judgment. Here the sea is "made of service" to people: put at their disposal so that ships can sail on it. "Seek of His bounty" is a phrase the Quran often uses for trade and earning a living.

posts.display: And We have commended unto man kindness toward parents. His mother beareth him with reluctance, and bringeth him forth with reluctance.
posts.display_original: وَوَصَّيْنَا ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ بِوَٰلِدَيْهِ إِحْسَٰنًا حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُۥ كُرْهًا وَوَضَعَتْهُ كُرْهًا
posts.caption: Al-Ahqaf, "The Wind-Curved Sandhills", is a Meccan surah of 35 verses. This is the opening of a longer verse on parents. "With reluctance" renders kurhan, which commentators explain as hardship and pain: what a mother endures in pregnancy and birth. The verse goes on to a prayer of thanks for the blessings given to oneself and one's parents.

Classical commentators connect this with a time when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was reciting the Quran in prayer at Nakhla, between Mecca and Ta'if. Jinn are unseen beings who, in Islamic belief, have free will like humans. "Give ear!" means "Listen in silence!", and these jinn went home to warn their own people.

This Medinan surah of 38 verses is named after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, whose name appears in its second verse. Knowing that there is no god but Allah comes first here, then seeking forgiveness for oneself and for all believers. Imam al-Bukhari cited this verse to show that knowledge comes before speech and action.

A short, pointed question. "Meditate" translates yatadabbarun, from the same root as tadabbur: reading the Quran slowly and thinking about what it means. The image of locks on the hearts suggests hearts shut so firmly that the words cannot get in.

posts.display: Lo! We have given thee (O Muhammad) a signal victory.
posts.caption: Al-Fath, "The Victory", is a Medinan surah of 29 verses. According to classical commentators it was revealed in 628 CE, on the way back from Hudaybiyyah, where the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had agreed a truce with the Quraysh instead of entering Mecca. Many saw the treaty as a setback; the surah calls it a clear victory.

Al-Hujurat, "The Private Apartments", is a Medinan surah of 18 verses, much of it about how people treat one another. This verse follows guidance on settling a quarrel between two groups of believers, and it grounds peacemaking in brotherhood: believers are one family.

posts.display: O ye who believe! Shun much suspicion; for lo! some suspicion is a crime. And spy not, neither backbite one another.
posts.display_original: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ ٱجْتَنِبُوا۟ كَثِيرًا مِّنَ ٱلظَّنِّ إِنَّ بَعْضَ ٱلظَّنِّ إِثْمٌ وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا۟ وَلَا يَغْتَب بَّعْضُكُم بَعْضًا
posts.caption: The opening of a verse on three habits that damage a community: suspicion, spying and backbiting (ghibah, speaking ill of someone behind their back). The verse goes on to compare backbiting to eating the flesh of one's dead brother, one of the Quran's most vivid images.

Addressed to all humanity, not only believers. Differences of nation and tribe exist so that people may come to know one another. "Best in conduct" renders atqakum, the most mindful of Allah (from taqwa), so honour is measured by character, not lineage.

Qaf is a Meccan surah of 45 verses, named after its opening letter. A hadith in Sahih Muslim reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ often recited it in his Friday sermon. This is one of the most quoted verses on Allah's closeness: nearer than the jugular vein, the great vein in the neck.

Near its end, Qaf returns to its central theme, the resurrection. Creating the heavens and the earth brought Allah no weariness, and earlier the surah asks, "Were We then worn out by the first creation?" For the One who made everything, raising the dead is no strain. Pickthall's "naught" means "nothing".

Adh-Dhariyat, "The Winnowing Winds", is a Meccan surah of 60 verses. Here signs of Allah are found in two places: the world outside and the self within. "Portents" is Pickthall's word for ayat, signs, the same word used for the verses of the Quran.

One of the most quoted verses on the purpose of life. Jinn and humans are named together because both are accountable for their choices. Worship here is understood broadly, as a whole life lived in awareness of Allah, and some early commentators explained it as "to know Me".

At-Tur, "The Mount" (Mount Sinai), is a Meccan surah of 49 verses. According to Sahih al-Bukhari, Jubayr ibn Mut'im, not yet a Muslim, heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ recite these verses in prayer and said his heart nearly flew. They ask simple questions about where we came from.

Comfort for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in hard years: "thou art in Our sight", watched over and protected. Many commentators link the praise "at the setting of the stars" with the prayers before dawn, and the night-time praise with prayers in the night.

posts.display: He is Best Aware of you (from the time) when He created you from the earth, and when ye were hidden in the bellies of your mothers. Therefor ascribe not purity unto yourselves. He is Best Aware of him who wardeth off (evil).
posts.display_original: هُوَ أَعْلَمُ بِكُمْ إِذْ أَنشَأَكُم مِّنَ ٱلْأَرْضِ وَإِذْ أَنتُمْ أَجِنَّةٌ فِى بُطُونِ أُمَّهَٰتِكُمْ فَلَا تُزَكُّوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُمْ هُوَ أَعْلَمُ بِمَنِ ٱتَّقَىٰٓ
posts.caption: An-Najm, "The Star", is a Meccan surah of 62 verses. These words close a longer verse: Allah has known each person since before birth, so no one is in a position to claim purity for themselves. "Him who wardeth off (evil)" is Pickthall's phrase for a person of taqwa, mindfulness of Allah.

posts.display: And that man hath only that for which he maketh effort, And that his effort will be seen. And afterward he will be repaid for it with fullest payment.
posts.caption: These lines come from a summary of teachings found in "the books of Moses and Abraham". Each person answers for their own effort, and that effort is seen and repaid in full. Pickthall's "maketh effort" translates sa'a: to strive or work toward something.

Al-Qamar, "The Moon", is a Meccan surah of 55 verses. Classical commentators, citing hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, understand this as a miracle seen in Mecca in the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: the moon split in two. Some read it instead as a sign of the Last Day.

This line returns four times in Al-Qamar, after stories of peoples who rejected their prophets. "Easy to remember" translates a word that also means easy to take as a reminder. Many Muslims see it reflected in how many people, children included, learn the whole Quran by heart.

posts.display_original: ٱلرَّحْمَٰنُ عَلَّمَ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ خَلَقَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ عَلَّمَهُ ٱلْبَيَانَ
posts.caption: Ar-Rahman, "The Most Merciful", has 78 verses and is sometimes called the "bride of the Quran" for its beauty. It opens with a name of Allah, and commentators note that teaching the Quran is mentioned even before creating man. "Utterance" renders al-bayan: clear speech.

Here the refrain that runs through Ar-Rahman appears for the first time; it comes 31 times in all. The "your" is dual in Arabic, addressing two audiences at once: humans and jinn. Each time it follows a gift or a sign, here the earth with its fruit, grain and fragrant herbs.

Everything on earth passes; only Allah remains. Pickthall's "Countenance" translates wajh, face. The title "of Might and Glory", dhul-jalali wal-ikram, returns in the surah's last verse, and Muslims often call on Allah by it in prayer.

Among the best-known lines of Ar-Rahman. "Goodness" here is ihsan, doing what is beautiful and excellent, which a famous hadith describes as worshipping Allah as if you see Him. The verse sits among descriptions of the gardens promised to those who stand in awe of their Lord.

Al-Waqi'ah, "The Event", is a Meccan surah of 96 verses describing the Day of Judgment and the three groups people will fall into. In its picture of Paradise one detail stands out: no idle or hurtful talk, only words of peace. The Arabic, salaman salama, repeats the word salam.

Part of a series of questions in Al-Waqi'ah about everyday things: seed, crops, water and fire. Each asks who is really behind what people take for granted. "Bitter" translates ujaj, salty and undrinkable like seawater, and the passage ends with a call to gratitude.

Al-Hadid, "Iron", is a Medinan surah of 29 verses, named after a later verse that mentions iron. This verse holds four names of Allah: al-Awwal, al-Akhir, az-Zahir and al-Batin, the First, the Last, the Outward and the Inward. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported to have used them in a prayer before sleep.

posts.display: Race one with another for forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whereof the breadth is as the breadth of the heavens and the earth.
posts.display_original: سَابِقُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ مَغْفِرَةٍ مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ وَجَنَّةٍ عَرْضُهَا كَعَرْضِ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ
posts.caption: An invitation to race, not for wealth but for forgiveness. It follows a verse comparing worldly life to plants that flourish after rain and then wither into straw. That closes this journey from As-Saffat to Al-Hadid; thank you for reading along.
